title: TB5-04533
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): XXXX XXXX (the "Appellant"), a citizen of Turkey, appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) that he is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX (the "Appellant"), a citizen of Turkey, appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) that he is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. He has further appealed a decision by the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) confirming the RPD's decision, and the Federal Court has remitted the matter to the RAD for reconsideration. The Appellant has submitted new evidence in support of his claim. He has not requested an oral hearing. The Appellant requests that the RAD set aside the determination of the RPD and find that he is a Convention refugee. Alternatively, the Appellant requests that the matter be remitted to the RPD for reconsideration by a differently constituted panel.

Pursuant to section 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), the RAD confirms the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. The appeal is dismissed. Background

The Appellant alleged in his Basis of Claim (BOC) form that he faces persecution in Turkey on the basis of his Armenian ethnicity, his Christian religion, his leftist political activities, including his involvement with the Freedom and Solidarity Party (øzg■rl■k ve Dayanisma Partisi - ODP), and his being a conscientious objector to military service. The Issues
The panel indicated the issues in regard to this claim are credibility and failure to claim elsewhere.

The Appellant submits that the issues in this appeal are the following: (a) whether the panel failed to consider documentary evidence relevant to the case; (b) whether the panel made vague, unreasonable and selective inferences from the evidence; (c) whether the panel's finding is implausible and inconsistent; (d) whether the panel's analysis on the issue of the XXXX XXXX protest is microscopic and ignores documentary evidence; (e) whether the panel ignored documentary evidence in support of the Appellant's claim of involvement with the ODP; (f) whether the panel erred in finding the Appellant had not provided sufficient credible evidence to establish his profile as a political activist who faced problems with authorities or his being a conscientious objector or his subjective fear of persecution due to his Armenian-Christian background. (g) whether the panel's decision, on the whole, is patently unreasonable. Credibility The Appellant's High School and University Documentation

The panel found that the Appellant was inconsistent about his school history in Turkey. The panel noted that the Appellant's testimony concerning when he graduated from high school, whether it was a regular or an open education high school and whether there was a difference as to military deferment between the two school systems. The panel noted that the Appellant's testimony differed from the information he provided in his IMM5669 form.1 The panel found the description of the Appellant's studies relevant as it related to the issue of military deferral and how his school was viewed by the military. The panel drew a negative inference from both the inconsistent timeline given for the Appellant's studies and his inconsistent description of his high school being viewed as part of the regular system or not.

The panel noted that the Appellant stated he stopped attending university in XXXX in XXXX 2014 after being attacked and threatened by nationalist students. The panel confirmed the date and then noted that the Appellant indicated in his IMM5669 form that he studied in XXXX until XXXX 2014.2 The Appellant explained that he did not attend school until June, but he was registered during that time. The panel rejected this explanation, as the question concerned his activities during this period, and the Appellant indicated in the IMM5669 form that he was living in XXXX from 2011 until XXXX 2014.3 The Appellant responded there must be a mistake because he was not in XXXX from 2011, but 2012.

The panel questioned the Appellant as to why he listed his address as being in XXXX until XXXX 2014, and he explained he did not think it was important, so he indicated XXXX as he was sometime in other cities. The panel drew a negative inference from the Appellant's inconsistent personal history, as it covered the period of the central allegations.

The panel noted that the Appellant provided no high school documentation, although he indicated that he had been given a document concerning his being thrown out of regular high school. The Appellant did provide a student ID certificate, transcript and student card from his university prior to the second sitting of the hearing. The panel noted, however, that no documentation was provided concerning the issues noted above, in particular when and where the Appellant was living and studying. The panel noted this information is linked to his military deferral. The panel drew a negative inference from the absence of what it considered to be reasonably available evidence.

The panel provided an analysis of the school documents disclosed by the Appellant and noted discrepancies that confirmed its credibility concerns. The panel noted that the transcript and student certificate4 indicates that the Appellant registered for his studies in XXXX 2012, but his student certificate, issued in XXXX 2008, lists him as in year one of two, and his transcript contains only one semester of marks. The panel further noted that the Appellant' student card,5 valid to 2017, is for the 2013/14 school year, which appears from the other documents to be the first year of the Appellant's university studies. The panel found that, while the Appellant may have registered in 2012, the evidence establishes that he did not attend university until the fall of 2013, and this is inconsistent with the Appellant's oral testimony that he started university in 2012 and his written statements6 that he studied in university since 2011.

The Appellant submits that the panel's negative credibility findings concerning his school and university documents and statements are baseless and unreasonable. The Appellant further submits that he was enrolled in and graduated from high school and continued his studies in XXXX University. The Appellant submits as well that whether he studied in an open or regular high school is irrelevant for the purpose of deferral of military service.

The Appellant submits that the panel misunderstood the linkage between the education system and military deferment. The Appellant cites country documentary evidence,7 which indicates that military service is compulsory for all males in Turkey, but that service can be deferred if a person is pursuing studies.

The Appellant submits that he completed his high school studies and was enrolled in XXXX University until the academic year 2013-2014, with a validity period to 2017. The Appellant further submits that whether he completed the degree program is not the issue. His status was that of a student until XXXX 2014.

The Appellant notes that the military letter, dated XXXX XXXX, 2010,8 was issued at the Appellant's request. The document was provided to show the link between student status and military deferment. The Appellant submits that, if the Appellant had requested an updated letter, it would have been provided.

The Appellant further submits that, assuming without admitting that the Appellant was not a student and/or was a military evader when he left Turkey, the fact that he got his passport in XXXX 2014 proves that his military service was deferred. The Appellant notes in this regard that the panel's reference to country documentary evidence indicates that it is practically impossible for a military evader to obtain a passport.

The Appellant submits that the panel over-complicated the timelines corroborating his student years. The Appellant argues that the dates he gave were estimates, and he should be given the benefit of the doubt.

The RAD has reviewed all of the evidence in the record concerning the Appellant's school timeline and its relationship to deferral of military service. The RAD is not persuaded by the Appellant's argument that the panel's concerns are baseless and unreasonable. The RAD notes that the panel's concerns are founded on the Appellant's inconsistent testimony and lack of clarity in the Appellant's evidence concerning his time in XXXX University. The RAD also notes that the Appellant stated in his BOC that his open high school did not automatically defer military service.9 The RAD finds that the panel did not err by drawing a negative inference from the Appellant's inconsistent testimony. Ability of the Appellant to Obtain a Passport and Leave Turkey

The Appellant testified that he had no difficulties in obtaining a passport and exiting Turkey. The panel noted in the hearing that country documentary evidence indicated that those with military issues are likely not able to obtain a passport and leave Turkey.10 The panel further noted that the Appellant was unable to explain his ability to leave Turkey in XXXX 2014, if his postponement expiration date was XXXX XXXX, 2013, as indicated in the military service document he provided. Counsel indicated in the hearing that there was another document that post-dated and superseded this document, but no such disclosure was provided.

The panel noted that the documents provided by the Appellant suggest his exemption expired on XXXX XXXX, 2013, and country documentary evidence indicates that military authorities maintain records concerning those who defer entrance into the military.11 The panel further noted that country documentary evidence indicates that those whose service is not in order cannot obtain a passport.12 The panel found it to be unlikely that the Appellant was able to obtain a passport if he was months past his deferral end date. The panel cited further country documentary evidence concerning border exit controls and the bar code on newer passports that provides information on a person's military service.13 The panel noted that the Appellant did not seem aware that he would have a problem obtaining a passport or that military information was contained in the passport. The panel found it reasonable to expect someone involved in the conscientious objector movement to know.

While counsel in the hearing noted that the Appellant's passport was valid for only one year, the panel noted that the passport validity can be selected by the applicant,14 with varying costs based on the duration of validity. The panel did not find this to be evidence of the Appellant's military service status. The panel found, in the context of the expiration of the Appellant's military deferral, that his ability to obtain a passport and exit the country was inconsistent with country documentary evidence. The panel also found that this further brings into question the Appellant's allegations as to his military service and deferral.

The panel noted its concerns about the Appellant's ability to obtain a passport and leave Turkey in the context of its further concerns regarding the Appellant's school history. The panel noted that the questions raised by the Appellant's supporting military documents and the documentary evidence, and it indicated that this aspect of the Appellant's personal history has not been established as to the link between the Appellant's studies and his military deferral. The panel found, though denied by the Appellant in the hearing, that he could reasonably have completed his military service in the time between completing his high school studies and beginning his university studies in the Fall of 2013.

The Appellant notes that the panel accepted the letter from the military office as proof of his student status and then made negative credibility findings on the basis of the letter. The Appellant further notes that the panel used the letter to conclude that his student status ended in 2013. The Appellant argues that if that were the case, the panel should have been aware that he could not have left Turkey in XXXX 2014 because he would still be in active service in XXXX 2014. The Appellant submits that the panel was selective in its reliance on the Appellant's documentary evidence to refute his claims.

The Appellant submits that the reason he had no difficulty in obtaining a passport and leaving Turkey was because he was still a student, and his military service was automatically deferred for the year 2013-14.

The RAD has reviewed all of the evidence concerning the military letter and the Appellant's military deferral. The RAD finds there is a lack of clarity in the evidence. The RAD notes that the Appellant has not provided documentation concerning his high school studies. In addition, the Appellant has stated in his BOC that he was called up for military examination while he was attending the open high school. He further stated that he did not cooperate with the doctor, and he was kicked out of his room, and subsequently the military started a proceeding against him. The Appellant then stated, "I knew that matter at the military courts takes [a] very long time and in the meantime I planned and studied hard to go to university."15

The RAD notes that the panel's suggestion as to whether the Appellant completed his military service between high school and university is not a firm finding but rather an indication of possibility. While the RAD further notes that the Appellant's argument that, if his student status ended in 2013, there was insufficient time between to obtain a passport because he would not have completed his military service; this does not account for the possibility of the Appellant completing his service before he attended university.

The RAD finds that, while there is insufficient evidence to support a finding that the Appellant completed his military service between high school and university, the panel's concerns in this regard remain unresolved. Failure to Make a Claim in the United States

The panel found it reasonable that, if the Appellant feared persecution in Turkey, he would have made a claim at the first opportunity in the United States, especially in the context of the risk of being caught at the Canadian border. The panel noted that the Appellant is educated, and he was able to obtain information regarding obtaining a visa to the United States, and it was reasonable to expect that he could find assistance to access information regarding the United States asylum system. The panel drew a negative inference as to the Appellant's subjective fear and the credibility of his allegations given his failure to make a claim in the United States and the risk he took in illegally crossing into Canada.

The Appellant submits that his cousin, a successful refugee claimant in Canada, gave him advice concerning his decision not to make a claim in the United States and to proceed to Canada. The Appellant further submits that he had a valid U.S. visa, and he was in no danger of deportation. The Appellant argues that the panel's negative inference in this regard does not take into consideration the situation noted above and his narrative.

The RAD has reviewed all of the evidence concerning the Appellant's failure to make a claim for refugee protection in the United States. The RAD notes that there is a substantial body of Federal Court jurisprudence concerning this issue. In Garzon, the Court stated that: The Applicant's submission that he did not apply for asylum because it would be granted more easily in Canada or because he would gain permanent residence faster in Canada are not valid reasons for negating the adverse inference that he lacked subjective fear by not applying for asylum in the United States.16

The RAD further cites the Court's decision in Gebetas,17 in which the Court rejected an explanation that the applicant wanted to make a claim in Canada because his sister was there. The Court stated: "This explanation, in the Court's view is an unacceptable reason to delay seeking asylum in another country and strongly indicates a lack of subjective fear of persecution."

In Assadi,18 the Court stated that the failure to immediately seek protection can impugn a claimant's credibility, including testimony about events in the claimant's country of origin. In addition, the Court, in Ilie,19 held that the tribunal was entitled to consider an applicant's failure to claim protection in other countries and consider as well how the applicant's evidence was to be weighed in light of that failure.

The RAD finds that there is no evidence that the panel did not consider the Appellant's explanation for not seeking protection in the United States. The RAD has reviewed the explanation that the Appellant's cousin is a successful refugee claimant in Canada and further finds, in the context of the Federal Court jurisprudence cited above, that the panel did not err in rejecting the explanation and drawing a negative inference as to the Appellant's subjective fear of persecution in Turkey The XXXX XXXX Protest

The panel noted that the Appellant indicated in his BOC that he attended a protest at his school on XXXX XXXX, 2012, commemorating the Armenian genocide and the killing of an Armenian soldier by a nationalist Turkish soldier. In oral testimony, however, the Appellant gave the date as XXXX XXXX, 2013. The panel noted that it confirmed the date with the Appellant and was about to put the inconsistency to the Appellant, when counsel interjected that the date in the BOC should have been amended from 2012 to 2013. The panel noted that the amendment should have been made at the outset of the hearing when the Appellant confirmed that the information in his BOC was complete, true and correct. Counsel responded that it was inadvertently missed. The panel noted that the matter was raised by counsel only after it became an issue in the hearing. The panel found that accepting counsel's late correction as it being an oversight did not explain why the date of 2012 was initially given in the BOC.

The Appellant stated that he and friends were beaten and detained during the protest, and the panel asked if the incident was reported locally. The Appellant said no because authorities "want to silence some of the incidents that took place".20 The panel cited country documentary evidence that stated: As in the previous year, the gatherings on XXXX XXXX to commemorate events relating to the Armenian issue and the tragic events of 1915 were peaceful and received police protection where necessary.21

The Appellant responded that that is how they mention it. The panel noted that this was not a Turkish report and that the details of arrests and violence at other protests were provided. The Appellant responded that Turkish authorities cover up things, and he did not know how the Americans find out these things.22 The panel found it reasonable that any incidents of this nature on such a sensitive date would be mentioned. The panel also noted that country reports were silent on such problems at XXXX XXXX protests in 2013 and found this further brought into question the Appellant's allegations. The panel found as well that the events of XXXX XXXX, 2013, alleged by the Appellant, did not occur as alleged.

The Appellant submits that the panel over-emphasized the date of the protest and argues that he inadvertently put the wrong date in his BOC. The Appellant notes that this was corrected in the hearing.

The Appellant further submits that the panel ignored substantial documentary evidence provided by the Appellant substantiating atrocities against Armenian Christians and focuses on only one document to refute his claim. The Appellant argues that the panel should have provided analysis of documentation supporting his claim. The Appellant further argues that the panel was selective in its citations of documentary evidence and did not refer to documentation which supports his claim.

The RAD notes, in regard to the inconsistency in the Appellant's testimony concerning the year of the XXXX XXXX protest, that counsel and not the Appellant gave testimony as to the different date in the Appellant's BOC, 2012 rather than 2013. The RAD notes that the Appellant confirmed at the beginning of the hearing that the information in the BOC was complete, true and correct.

The RAD has reviewed all of the evidence in the record, including country documentary evidence concerning the XXXX XXXX protest. The RAD notes that the Appellant provided no reference to documentary evidence concerning arrests and detentions as a result of the XXXX XXXX, 2012 protest. In addition, the RAD finds no such evidence in the record.

The RAD finds, on the basis of its review of the evidence in the record, that it was open to the panel to find that the events of XXXX XXXX, 2013, as alleged by the Appellant, did not occur. The Appellant's Involvement with the ODP

The panel noted that the Appellant indicated in his IMM5669 form that he was a supporter of the ODP from XXXX 2008 until XXXX 2014 in Turkey.23 The Appellant was questioned in the hearing as to when he began his involvement with the party, and he stated, between 2009 and 2010 and indicated that he was just guessing. The panel noted that he indicated the start date as 2008 in his IMM5669 form, and the Appellant responded that this could be true, as he was only making an estimation at the time, and he was not good at dates. The panel found the start date of the Appellant's political activities to be sufficiently significant that it was reasonable he would have recalled it. The panel drew a negative inference in this regard and with his inconsistent testimony concerning his start date with the ODP.

The panel noted that the Appellant provided a copy of a letter from the ODP-XXXX Province in support of his claim.24 The panel further noted that the Appellant indicated in the first sitting of the hearing that he would be able to obtain the original from his father, but no such documentation was provided.

The panel asked the Appellant when the XXXX branch of the ODP was established. The Appellant responded that he did not know, but he met them while he was in high school, so it was obviously established before then. The panel noted that the ODP letter indicated that the Appellant had participated in the party's work since the XXXX branch was established. The panel asked the Appellant when the branch was established, and he responded that he did not know. The panel noted that the Appellant was able to provide the correct start date for the establishment of the ODP in Turkey. It further noted that the Appellant was able to recall some dates with accuracy, although not dates from his own personal experiences. In the context of the concerns noted above, the lack of the original document and the unavailability of the writer for questioning by the panel, the panel gave the ODP letter little weight.

The Appellant notes that the ODP letter was given little weight because he could not recall the years of his involvement with the party, because the letter is not an original, and the writer was not available for examination. The Appellant argues that it is ridiculous to assume that the writer of the party membership letter would come to Canada for the hearing. The Appellant further argues that there is no point in writing a letter if one is expected to be examined as to its contents. The Appellant submits that the letter has a business address, an ODP logo, a seal and signature of the party president. The letter was issued to confirm his membership and affiliation with the OPD. The Appellant further submits that the panel ignored the fact that he was a member of the ODP.

The RAD has reviewed all of the evidence concerning the Appellant's support of and membership in the ODP. The RAD notes that the Appellant's testimony regarding when he became associated with the ODP was vague and inconsistent. The RAD further notes that the letter from the ODP also lacked specificity about when the Appellant started his association with the ODP. The RAD finds, in the context of the analysis above, that the panel did not err in giving the ODP letter little weight. The Appellant's Alleged Risk Profile Church Involvement in Turkey and Canada

The Appellant indicated that he did not have the opportunity to practice his faith in Turkey, as there was no church in his area. The Appellant further indicated that, when he was in Istanbul, he did not attend a church service because they were held early on Sunday mornings, and he was still sleeping. The panel found the Appellant's testimony establishes that he was not prevented from practising his faith but that he made little effort to do so. The panel noted that the Appellant made little effort to practice his faith in Canada. The panel noted that the Appellant provided a letter25 from a church in Canada that does not identify him as a Christian. The letter indicates that they have no idea about his personal life, just that he attends from time to time and likes to listen to the word of God. The panel accepted that the Appellant is of Armenian Christian descent, based on the sworn testimony of his cousin.26 The panel did not find that the Appellant is a practising Christian or that he is actively interested in pursuing his faith. The Appellant's Political Profile

The panel accepted that the Appellant may well be a supporter of the ODP and leftist political ideology and platform. On the basis of its findings above, the panel did not find that he experienced the problems he alleged related to his political opinion and activities.

The panel reviewed both the National Documentation Package (NDP) documentation and documents provided by the Appellant.27 The panel found that as a general supporter of the ODP, the Appellant has not established the harm he fears related to his political opinion or activities. The panel noted that the ODP is not viewed as a significant threat by Turkish authorities due to its small size and anti-violence stance. The panel acknowledged that a recent Response to Information Request (RIR) indicates that members of the ODP are often harassed by Turkish authorities, but that the panel noted that the Appellant did not allege he was a member of the ODP. The panel noted the lack of specific mention in country documentation of general supporters of the ODP being targeted by authorities in Turkey or that they generally face harm because of their involvement in the party.

The panel accepted that the Appellant may well be a general supporter of the ODP and leftist politics, as are tens of thousands of others in Turkey. The panel found, however, that the Appellant had not established, on a balance of probabilities, his profile beyond a low level supporter of the party, and that he is not a leader, a member or an activist. The panel found that the Appellant's evidence did not establish his profile as an ODP activist or that his political activity would attract the attention of the authorities. The panel further found that the Appellant's political profile is not such that he would face a risk described in ss. 96 or 97 of the IRPA. The Appellant's Profile as an Armenian Christian

The panel did not find in the evidence that the Appellant would face a risk of harm under ss. 96 and 97 as a result of his Armenian Christian identity. The panel acknowledged that country reports indicate that discrimination is faced by minority groups. The panel found, however, that the documentary evidence does not indicate that Armenian Christians face systemic targeting, societal discrimination and harassment that rises to the level of persecution. The panel cited country documentary evidence that indicated that Armenian language newspapers are published, and radio and television programs are broadcast in Armenian in Turkey.28

The panel noted reports on the 2007 murder of a Turkish-Armenian journalist and the death of a Turkish-Armenian soldier in 2011. The panel further noted that these incidents were investigated and taken before the courts. The panel noted as well the fact that these incidents are still cited in reports on Armenians in Turkey suggests that such incidents are not the norm and have not occurred in the years after 2011.

The panel acknowledged 2013 news articles disclosed by the Appellant regarding a series of attacks on Armenian Christian women in Istanbul. Some articles indicated robbery was the motive while others indicated the motive was religion. The panel noted that these appeared to be isolated incidents with little to suggest the risk is ongoing or that it had extended generally to Armenian Christians in Turkey.

The panel noted that much of counsel's submissions in this regard relied on a 46-page report29 apparently from 2002, with most of the sources cited from the 1990s. The panel further noted that the report indicates something coming up in 2003, in the future tense. The panel acknowledged the usefulness of the historical background but indicated its preference for more recent documentation.

The panel noted that Armenian Orthodox Christians are among three groups granted special legal minority status in Turkey. They have the right to practice their faith freely and openly. The panel cited country documentary evidence30 which states that Armenian Orthodox communities in Turkey reported they had the freedom to practice their faiths. The panel acknowledged there were reports of abuses of religious freedom but found little evidence to suggest that Armenian Christians generally face problems or treatment that would amount to persecution.
In the context of the analysis above, the panel found that the Appellant has not established his fear of persecution or other harm as an Armenian Christian in Turkey.

The Appellant submits that the panel erred in finding that the Appellant has not provided sufficient credible and trustworthy evidence to establish his profile as a political activist who has faced problems with authorities or his being a conscientious objector or his subjective fear of persecution due to his Armenian-Christian background.

The Appellant submits that he is of Armenian Christian descent but has been forcibly converted to Islam. He further submits that he does not have rights as an Armenian, but he is still viewed as an Armenian even though he is not recognized as such. The Appellant further submits that his case is different from other Armenians, and even if this is not so, the panel ignored volumes of country documentation concerning atrocities committed on Armenians, Christians and practically all ethnic and religious minorities in Turkey by the police.

The Appellant submits that the panel erred in ignoring the 46-page document on the situation of Armenians in Turkey.31 The Appellant notes the historical significance of the document. The Appellant further notes that there is continuing persecution reflected in 2013 news reports. The Appellant argues the panel erred in law by selectively relying on some documentation and not referring to documentary evidence that supports his claim.

The RAD has reviewed all of the evidence in the record concerning the Appellant's political and religious identity, including country documentary evidence in the NDP and further documentary evidence provided by the Appellant. The RAD is not persuaded by the Appellant's argument.

The RAD finds that whether the Appellant is a member of the ODP or only a supporter, there is no evidence in the record that he has played a leadership or significant activist role that would cause him to be targeted by the authorities. The RAD further finds that the Appellant may have experienced problems with the authorities, including a brief detention, as a result of his participation in protests, but these experiences do not rise to the level of persecution.

The RAD notes that country documentary evidence indicates that the police in Turkey have responded, sometimes aggressively, to protests against the government and that participants in protests, whatever their political or ethnic background or the particular issue that caused them to protest, have been abused and detained merely as members of the protesting group.

The RAD notes, as an example, the massive protest in opposition to the redevelopment of XXXX XXXX in Istanbul. The RAD further notes that the Appellant was also involved in the XXXX XXXX protest which did not concern an ODP priority or an Armenian issue. Thousands of people came out in Istanbul and other cities to protect the park from a redevelopment plan embraced by the president. Country documentary evidence32 indicates that security forces used excessive force in response to the protest, detainees were held for long periods, and there were as well extended trials. The RAD notes that the Appellant stated in his BOC that he was detained overnight.

The RAD notes that country documentary evidence indicates the 2011 elections were free and fair.33 The RAD further notes that, in September 2013, the government proposed lowering the threshold for state funding for political parties from 7 percent of the votes to 3 percent of the votes, which benefits smaller parties such as the BDP.34

The RAD concurs with the panel's finding that the Appellant has failed to establish a political profile that would lead to personal targeting by the authorities, a risk of persecution or a risk of harm as indicated in s. 97 of the IRPA.

The RAD acknowledges that Armenian Christians have been persecuted in Turkey in the past, and Armenians continue to be subject to prejudice and harassment. The RAD finds that country documentary evidence indicates that the serious problems reflected in the historical document35 disclosed by the Appellant does not inform the current situation. The RAD notes, as did the panel, that there have been serious incidents such as the murder of the Armenian journalist, Hirant Dink in 2007, the killing of an Armenian soldier by a Turkish nationalist soldier in 2011 and the 2013 attacks on three Armenian women.

The RAD agrees with the panel that there is no evidence that these incidents reflect a broad-based risk of persecution for Armenian Christians generally. The RAD notes that country documentary evidence indicates that those responsible for the murder of Hirant Dink have been tried and convicted. The man who was found to be the instigator was sentenced to life in prison, and three others received sentences of two months to ten years.36 The perpetrators of the other incidents have also been brought to court.

The RAD further notes that, as a result of a Constitutional Court ruling that the government's investigation of the Dink murder was inadequate and the rights of the Dink family were violated, the government launched negligence cases against the police involved. As a result, two police officers turned themselves in as well as the Cizre police chief. In addition, the former chief of the Police Intelligence Bureau was detained. This information is included in the most recent NDP.37

The RAD notes that no evidence was provided in the Appellant's BOC or in oral testimony that he was forcibly converted to Islam. Rather, the evidence indicates that he did not attend a church because there was none in the towns where he lived, and he demonstrated little interest in attending church when one was available.

The RAD further notes, as did the panel, that country documentary evidence states: As in the previous year, the gatherings on XXXX XXXX to commemorate events relating to the Armenian issue and the tragic events of 1915 were peaceful and received police protection where necessary.38

The RAD has reviewed all of the country documentary evidence in the record, including the evidence provided by the Appellant, concerning the situation of Armenian Christians in Turkey at this time. The RAD has acknowledged that Armenian Christians continue to be subject to prejudice and harassment but finds, as did the panel, that this treatment does not rise to the level of persecution. Armenian Christians are able to practice their faith freely, and their religion is one of three non-Muslim traditions recognized by the state.

The RAD concurs with the panel's finding that the Appellant has not established that he is at risk of persecution or of harm indicated in s. 97 of the IRPA as a result of his Armenian Christian identity. Conscientious objector

The panel found that, even if the Appellant had not completed his military service and was still required to do so after his studies, this in itself does not establish his claim. The panel noted that, although the Appellant alleged that he was involved in a conscientious objector group in Turkey, he had initially provided no corroborating evidence in this regard. The panel further noted that, at the end of the first sitting of the hearing, the Appellant was asked to provide emails from his time with the group and from his time of joining the group for the second sitting. At the second sitting, no such documents were provided. The Appellant explained that he had forwarded a number of emails, but counsel determined that it was too much to print and have translated.

The panel requested that this documentation be provided post-hearing. The panel indicated that the full content of the emails need not be included, but the "header" information should be provided: sender, recipient, date, subject line; and that these should cover the timespan of the Appellant's involvement with the group. The panel noted that, while some emails39 were provided post-hearing, these were dated from after the first sitting, and they did not give any indication of the Appellant's involvement with the group during his time in Turkey.

The panel found, as these documents were not from the time the Appellant was in Turkey and allegedly registered with the group, that the documentary evidence does not establish the Appellant's involvement with the group in Turkey, as alleged, but rather suggests that his involvement began after this issue was raised at the first sitting and, as such, appeared to have been done to buttress the claim.
In the context of the analysis above, the panel did not find, on a balance of probabilities, the Appellant to be a conscientious objector.

The Appellant submits that the issue of conscientious objection is subjective and cannot be viewed objectively. The Appellant further submits that the Appellant being of Armenian Christian descent has every right to object to serve in the military which was involved in the widely known genocide of his ancestors. The Appellant argues that having established his Armenian Christian background, the panel should have considered the issue of objection to service from this perspective.

The RAD has reviewed all of the evidence concerning the Appellant's allegation that he is a conscientious objector. The RAD is not persuaded that the Appellant's alleged identity as a conscientious objector cannot be viewed objectively. The RAD agrees with the panel that the Appellant has failed to provide convincing evidence concerning his association with a group that advocates conscientious objection to military service.

The RAD has considered the Appellant's identity as an Armenian Christian as a basis for his alleged conscientious objection to military service. The RAD rejects this argument as it is clear from the evidence that the Appellant is not a practising Christian. The RAD also rejects the argument that the genocidal attack on Armenian Christians almost one hundred years ago is a sufficient basis on which to find that the Appellant is a conscientious objector. The RAD finds there is insufficient evidence of a religious, ethnic or moral basis to support the Appellant's allegation in this regard. The Panel's Conclusions as to the Credibility of the Appellant

The panel found, on the basis of the cumulative negative inferences noted above, that the Appellant is generally not credible. The panel further found that the Appellant has not established, on a balance of probabilities, the factual basis for his fear that he would be persecuted or harmed in Turkey. The panel found that the Appellant's story as a whole lacked the ring of truth. The Appellant's Risk of Harm if he were to Return to Turkey

The Appellant argues that, even today, persons belonging to religious and ethnic minorities in Turkey are discriminated against and persecuted. The Appellant further argues that the panel failed to consider the issue of treatment of draft evaders in the Turkish military. The Appellant submits that the panel erred by failing to consider relevant evidence and to assess the evidence as a whole in a s. 97 analysis. The Appellant cites in this regard the decision of the Federal Court in Fixgera, in which the Court stated: [27] ... that there may be instances where a refugee claimant, whose identity is not disputed, is found to be not credible with respect to his subjective fear of persecution, but the country conditions are such that the claimant's particular circumstances make him/her a person in need of protection.40

The RAD notes that military service for a period of one year is mandatory in Turkey. The RAD finds therefore that this is a law of general application and raises the question of whether refusal to comply with the law would result in prosecution or persecution. The RAD further notes that Turkey does not recognize the right to conscientious objection to military service, and the penalties for evading the draft may not be revoked for religious or moral reasons.

The RAD notes, as indicated above, that there have been numerous human rights abuses in Turkey. Having found that the Appellant is not a conscientious objector and that he simply wishes to evade required military service in Turkey, the RAD needs to consider whether the Appellant would personally face a risk to his life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or a danger of torture upon his return to Turkey, in his particular situation and circumstance.

Country documentary evidence41 indicates that the penalty for draft evasion is a prison term, the length of which depends on the length of the delay in complying with the law. It is further noted that there are reports that conscripts were subject to "ill treatment". There is no evidence in this document, however, that indicates that the Appellant's Armenian Christian identity or his association with an opposition party would make him a particulate target of abuse.

The RAD notes that the Federal Court has held that when conscription for a legitimate and lawful purpose is conducted in a discriminatory way or the punishment for evasion is biased in relationship to a Convention ground, this may provide a nexus with a Convention ground.42 The RAD finds that, as a conscript, he may be at risk of some abuse like all other conscripts but that the abuse does not rise to the level indicated in either s. 96 or s. 97 of the IRPA.

The RAD further finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the Appellant would not be subject to a risk to his life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or a risk of torture if he were to return to Turkey and fulfil his obligation in Turkish law to serve in the army for one year. Admissibility of New Evidence Submitted on Appeal

Section 110(4) of the IRPA provides that the Appellant may present only evidence that arose after the rejection of his/her claim or that was not reasonably available, or that he/she could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented, at the time of the rejection of the claim.

The Appellant submits the RPD's decision in the case of XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX, dated 2 July 2015.43 The Appellant explains the relevance of this evidence, that the claimants are his cousins, and the grounds of their claims are based on facts that are similar to his claim. The Appellant further submits that this decision was not available to him at the time of his RPD hearing, and it came to his notice only recently.

The RAD has reviewed this document in the context of the statutory requirements noted above. The RAD finds this document was not reasonably available to the Appellant before the determination of the RPD in his case. The document is therefore admitted as new evidence.

The RAD has reviewed and assessed this new evidence and finds in the case at bar, unlike the findings in the case provided above as new evidence,, that there is no evidence that the Appellant was unable to practice his religion in Turkey because of any action by the state, or that he was particularly targeted as a result of his membership in the ODP and his support for the issues advocated by the party, or that he is a conscientious objector. The RAD's analysis and decisions noted above are founded on the distinctive evidence in the case at bar.

Pursuant to section 111(1)(a) of the IRPA, the RAD confirms the determination of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. The appeal is dismissed.
